doc.title: Christine Jensen interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, March 4, 2024

title: Conducting large ensembles
summary: She says her big band music does not always need a conductor, comparing Brookmeyer, McNeely and Basie, and describes her cross-Canada tour.

story.theme_name: Playing with Count Basie: joining, leading, leaving
story.community_name: Playing with Count Basie: the band, its feel and its people

blocks.x: Wow. Very interesting. Does your music, especially for large ensembles, really need to have a conductor?

Not always, no. And I’m noticing that too with a lot of that, the Brookmeyer stuff, I’m really caught up in like oh I can see what happens. He started to get really into the composer side of things, not sitting in the band, and then all of a sudden the Vanguard band, how are they going to run this episodic piece, that — someone has to direct it. Same with McNeely — has to direct it from the piano. And there’s just little cues. And so that might be something that you kind of keep in your tool kit as one of the actions happening in the piece because you want to play on it or you don’t want to be conducting. The other action that happens to me with my students is that they get so good at the music I don’t need to stand there anymore. Right? If they’re well rehearsed and the piece goes by I barely need to be there. However, if I am going to be there I’m hoping to give them

some energy. Like Ray Wright — I don’t know, or sorry, Ray Ricker — Ray Wright’s dead. Ray Ricker was at a concert, or he watched a concert the other night and he wrote me a note and he said, “I love your minimalistic conducting. It’s not like you’re like the wind symphony conductors where you have to direct everything.” And I said, “You don’t need to direct everything in jazz.” I mean it depends on context a lot but if the rhythm keeps the pulse of what’s going on, and it’s well rehearsed, you barely have to do anything. All you can do is throw good energy at it, at a certain point, which is what the great conductors were able to do because they had such great orchestras that knew the repertoire as far as I’m concerned. You know.
Yeah. Basie at the piano just like —

Yeah. He was barely doing anything he was just like one-two-three-four off you go. And yeah, I think the jazz repertoire for large ensemble is evolving all the time rhythmically and you know using different meters and things. So it gets complicated. It’s all time and place and what are we going to do. But I have to say when I took my band on tour, the one opportunity I got to go across Canada, by day three I did not need to stand in front of that band so I just started picking up my horn and playing melodies with them, or taking some solos, but it wasn’t about me soloing it was about just making the music — having fun with the music in the moment, which I hope happened.
